analysis.one_liner: Limits the mandatory overtime hours hospitals can force nurses to work.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals, home health agencies, and other Medicare-participating providers could no longer require nurses to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, or more than 12 hours straight, with a required 10-hour rest after a 12-hour shift. Nurses who refuse or report illegal overtime would be protected from retaliation, providers would have to post notices and document any emergency overtime, and repeat violators could face federal penalties. Voluntary overtime stays legal, and the limits can be lifted during declared emergencies and disasters.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses — registered, licensed practical, and licensed vocational — gain enforceable limits on forced overtime, a guaranteed rest period after 12-hour shifts, and protection from retaliation for refusing or reporting illegal overtime. Patients also benefit, because the bill's findings cite research linking long nurse hours to fatigue and medical errors.

how_it_helps.text: Bars hospitals and other Medicare-participating providers from requiring nurses to work beyond a previously scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, or more than 12 consecutive hours in a day, and requires a 10-hour rest period after a 12-hour stretch.
Protects nurses from firing, discipline, or retaliation for refusing illegal mandatory overtime or reporting violations, and lets them file complaints to HHS with investigations required.
Imposes civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with higher penalties for repeat offenders and public listing of penalized providers on an HHS website.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, surgical centers, home health agencies, and other Medicare-participating providers bear the cost: they lose the ability to force nurses past scheduled shifts, must document and post notices, and face civil penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation. Taxpayers fund the required federal studies.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals facing chronic understaffing lose the ability to require nurses to stay past scheduled shifts, and could have to refuse admissions, transfer patients, or leave unfilled shifts during shortages outside a declared emergency.

The emergency exception only lifts limits for formal declared disasters, so a localized staffing crisis that does not meet a declaration threshold gets no relief, and mandatory overtime beyond a scheduled shift is prohibited even if a nurse would prefer the pay.

Enforcement depends on the Health and Human Services Secretary investigating complaints and imposing penalties, so its real-world strength would rest on an administration's willingness to police hospitals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and well-documented in the bill's own findings: fatigue-driven medical errors harm patients and burn out nurses. The main cost is real — hospitals facing chronic understaffing lose the ability to compel nurses past 12 hours, and in true emergencies staffing gaps could force cancelled care until substitutes are found. The bill's emergency exception with documented good-faith staffing efforts is a reasonable safeguard, though the paperwork and penalty exposure adds compliance burden. On balance the safety and worker-protection gains outweigh the operational cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — and neither has taken it up, so it has never advanced toward a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Doris Matsui introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, joined by Representative Jennifer Kiggans of Virginia as the sole Republican cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day, a step most bills never get past.
No hearing, markup, or floor action appears in the record; the Congress ends January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained or lost; hospitals are spared any new restrictions because the bill has not moved, and nurses remain without federal overtime limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, so far — the bill went nowhere

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan but tiny: a Democratic sponsor, one Republican cosponsor, and three additional cosponsors in a 435-member House, with no committee action from either party.

industries.industry: Hospitals and Medicare-participating providers (hospitals, surgical centers, home health agencies, clinics)
industries.note: They lose the ability to force nurses past scheduled shifts or 12-hour days and face penalties and documentation requirements, but the bill also applies nationally a standard 18 states already have and still allows voluntary overtime and emergencies. For patients and the public, the effect is safer care from rested nurses.

industries.industry: Nurses (registered nurses, licensed practical and vocational nurses)
industries.note: The bill directly caps mandatory overtime, requires a 10-hour rest period after 12-hour shifts, protects nurses who complain from retaliation, and mandates posted schedules and rights notices. For the public, that means more alert caregivers and fewer fatigue-related errors.

analysis.trajectory: With two committees holding it, no hearing, a handful of cosponsors, and only about two months left in the session, the near-certain path is that the bill dies quietly at the end of this Congress unless a committee schedules it, which similar nurse-overtime proposals rarely get.
